description:
Machine learning, biomedical and developer expertise go well together in our team!
We're high school and uni students who want to make a difference for women's health in space and on Earth.
summary:
The current strategy for managing menstruation in space is... suppressing it with hormonal contraception. Every month the female body hands over a tissue sample for free, with no needle and it goes in the bin. Only about one in eight people who have flown to space are women, so almost everything space medicine knows comes from male bodies. For the crews now being selected for the Moon and Mars missions, a whole part of health goes unmonitored.

SpotOn is a health-monitoring system that uses the menstrual blood's full health monitoring potential. Each astronaut's molecular data from their menstrual blood is compared against her own terrestrial cycle history. Based on that, SpotOn generates a user-friendly risk and anomaly report with an option to chat about it with SI, ask follow up questions and export data for a check-up with a medical professional. 

SpotOn serves as an early health warning system suitable for long-term missions with female astronauts, but also for affected female communities on Earth, such as female athletes or women in rural areas.
details:
HOW IT WORKS: On Earth we build a reference from open datasets of donated menstrual blood, and within it we measure the thing the project rests on: how much a healthy woman naturally varies from one cycle to the next. Nobody has published that number, and without it any alert is meaningless, because you cannot tell a real change from ordinary monthly variation. In orbit, an astronaut collects one cup sample per cycle, sequences it on board, and is compared against her own previous months rather than against an average woman, since any individual would look abnormal simply for being herself. The output is a score from 0 to 100 for how unusual this month is, plus a readable explanation of what changed.

BENEFITS: It gives flight surgeons an early warning for a part of crew health that is currently unmeasured, from a sample that costs nothing to collect. It runs on board, so it needs no connection to Earth - which matters at Mars distance. And the normal-variation measurement is directly reusable by endometriosis and menstrual health research on Earth. Most astronauts currently suppress their periods in orbit, so SpotOn is not built for six-month Station flights. It is built for the missions where suppression stops being the easy answer: years long, with no resupply, no evacuation and a doctor who is minutes of signal delay away. On those missions a crew cannot react to a problem once it is obvious. It has to see it coming, and a monthly sample compared against the astronaut’s own history is a prediction tool, not a diagnosis.

TOOLS: Python with open single-cell and AI libraries (PyTorch, scanpy), open tools for Nanopore sequencing data, packaged with Docker so the identical analysis runs on a laptop, in the cloud, or in orbit. Flight hardware is a portable Oxford Nanopore sequencer. Code on GitHub.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE: We use a sample medicine discards. We could not train a computer to recognise "unhealthy in space" because no such sample has ever been collected, so we taught it only what normal looks like - and measuring that normal range is itself a new scientific result. And the sequencer has already run on the Space Station for six months without losing performance, so the flight half rests on proven hardware.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED: We have no sample from space yet; everything else exists, that one piece does not. Spaceflight changes several things at once, so we report how unusual a result is, not why. We built the reference from the same kind of sample we would actually collect (blood), rather than from larger but mismatched tissue datasets - a bigger dataset of the wrong tissue makes the model worse, not better.
